Adverbial Clauses: Reduced and Unreduced

Using adverbial clauses makes your speech and writing sound more dynamic and sophisticated.
When you want to express your ideas in a more concise way, you can shorten an adverbial clause to an adverbial phrase.
When you want to describe how something happens or is done, you can use adverbial clauses of manner.

Example:
Being adventurous, I wandered miles and miles.

You use adverbial clauses of time to show when something happens.

Example:
I wandered miles and miles along it after leaving the tour in the morning.

Adverbial clauses of comparison of degree answer the questions how much, how little or how many?

Example:
I have never been more elated and more tired than at that moment.

For example: I always take a shower before I go to bed.
Before going to bed, I always take a shower.

Present Perfect vs. Simple Past

You use the Present Perfect tense and the Simple Past tense to refer to past events.
The Present Perfect tense refers to actions that happened in the past and have some connection to the present.
The Simple Past passive focuses on the person or things which received a completed past action.

The Present Perfect tense refers to events that happened very recently. In these cases, you use words like just, only just and recently.
I have only just returned from a tour there.
You can use the Present Perfect in questions to ask about past experience or unusual events:

For example:
Have you ever been to the Great Wall of China?

Notice the use of the word ever in questions.

You also use words such as yet , up to now, so far and until now when you use the Present Perfect , since these words and phrases refer to a period of time covering the past to the present.

For example:
How many have considered trying to walk the 6000 km wall up to now?

Have you packed your bag yet?

(You use yet in negative statements and in questions).

The Simple Past Passive reports about events.
You use the passive form of the Simple Past when the action is not done by the subject but rather to the subject. Often, it is not known who has done the action.

For example:
I'm sure they were not moved easily.

The structure of the Simple Past Passive is:

subject + was/were + past participle
It has just been voted one of the new wonders of the word.
Starting in the 7th century, the walls have been and rebuilt until fairly recently.
So far, in modern times, people have only made it a few miles.
I'm sure they were not moved easily.
Over the years, the walls watch towers, troop barracks were erected and other modifications were done.
The path along the wall was constructed to be like a stone paved road.
Perhaps this was accomplished by sturdier Chinese soldiers of yore.

images.text: Have you ever been to the Great Wall of China? Is it on your bucket list? It has just been voted one of the new wonders of the world. The Chinese built this fortification of stone, brick, tampered earth and other materials to protect their states against raids. Starting in the 7th century, the walls have been built and rebuilt until fairly recently.

I have only just returned from a tour there. The huge stone slabs are impressive. How did workers bring them to the site? I'm sure they were not moved easily. They made as large an edifice as anywhere on Earth!

Over the years, watchtowers and troop barracks were erected and other modifications were done. The path along the wall was constructed to be like a paved road. Today, you can enjoy the view while winding through the stunning countryside.

Being adventurous, I wandered miles and miles along it after leaving the tour in the morning. Was this not more breathtaking than any historic site I had been to? Despite wanting to continue on, I returned to my hotel to soak my aching legs. I have never been more elated and more tired than at that moment.

Up to now, how many have considered trying to walk the 6000 km wall? Few I would say. Perhaps this was accomplished by sturdier Chinese soldiers of yore. So far, in modern times, people have only made it a few miles. If you haven't thought about trying this up to now, think it over. It may just turn out to be the walk a lifetime.
